arXiv:2509.02855v1 [cs.CL] 02 Sep 2025

IDEAlign: Comparing Large Language Models to Human Experts in
Open-ended Interpretive Annotations

Hyunji Nam    Lucia Langlois    James Malamut    Mei Tan    Dorottya Demszky Affiliation: Stanford University Affiliation: Correspondence:hjnam@stanford.edu Github : https://github.com/EduNLP/IDEAlign
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to open-ended, interpretive annotation tasks—such as thematic analysis by researchers or generating feedback on student work by teachers. These tasks involve free-text annotations requiring expert-level judgments grounded in specific objectives (e.g., research questions or instructional goals). Evaluating whether LLM-generated annotations align with those generated by expert humans is challenging to do at scale, and currently, no validated, scalable measure of similarity in ideas exists. In this paper, we (i) introduce the scalable evaluation of interpretive annotation by LLMs as a critical and understudied task, (ii) propose IDEAlign, an intuitive benchmarking paradigm for capturing expert similarity ratings via a pick-the-odd-one-out triplet judgment task, and (iii) evaluate various similarity metrics—including vector-based ones (topic models, embeddings) and LLM-as-a-judge via IDEAlign—against these human benchmarks. Applying this approach to two real-world educational datasets (interpretive analysis and feedback generation), we find that vector-based metrics largely fail to capture the nuanced dimensions of similarity meaningful to experts. Prompting LLMs via IDEAlign significantly improves alignment with expert judgments (9–30% increase) compared to traditional lexical and vector-based metrics. These results establish IDEAlign as a promising paradigm for evaluating LLMs against open-ended expert annotations at scale, informing responsible deployment of LLMs in education and beyond.

1 Introduction

Comparing machine predictions to human labels has long been central to ML evaluation. When outputs are categorical, assessing machine-learning or large language model (LLM) predictions is relatively straightforward  (Angelopoulos et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024; Strachan et al., 2024; Bojić et al., 2025; Schroeder and Wood-Doughty, 2025). By contrast, LLMs are increasingly used to generate open-ended text responses, which are harder to evaluate against human-generated responses  (Ismayilzada et al., 2025; Spangher et al., 2024; Muñoz-Ortiz et al., 2024; Wiegreffe et al., 2022). For instance, in education LLM-based tools like KhanMigo and Brisk observe student thinking and writing to provide insights to students and teachers (e.g., responding to their reasoning or offering feedback)  (Wen et al., 2024; Graesser et al., 2004; Khan, 2023; Team et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b). Because these open-ended, interpretive outputs can shape instruction, learning, and motivation, a rigorous evaluation of LLMs is essential. Doing so is nontrivial: the tasks require domain knowledge (e.g., standards and learning objectives), pedagogical expertise, and contextual understanding, and there is rarely a single “correct” response.

One important step toward evaluating—and ultimately improving—LLMs on such tasks is to assess their alignment with human experts at the level of ideas: the extent to which they express same underlying interpretations or suggested actions as experts, rather than sharing surface features (tone, length, phrasing). Measuring idea-level similarity is difficult for two reasons. First, expert annotations legitimately vary even when they agree on substance. Second, absolute, continuous similarity ratings are cognitively demanding and yield noisy, hard-to-calibrate labels. These challenges motivate an evaluation approach that elicits reliable relative judgments and validates automated similarity measures against them.

Existing evaluations of open-ended annotations typically rate responses along predefined dimensions (e.g., creativity (Ismayilzada et al., 2025; Spangher et al., 2024), power-affirmingness (Tan et al., 2024) and truthfulness (Lin et al., 2021)) or collect human preferences/rankings among model outputs (Wiegreffe et al., 2022). While these approaches capture certain aspects of quality and human values, they lack a flexible measure of similarity grounded in ideas. Automated text comparison metrics have complementary limitations: lexical overlap (e.g., BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002b)) ignores paraphrase; embedding-based  (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019; Radford et al., 2019; Greene et al., 2022; Neelakantan et al., 2022) and topic-based measures  (Grootendorst, 2022; Blei et al., 2001) conflate content with style/length and offer limited control over the dimension of comparison; and LLM-as-a-judge of similarity  (Zheng et al., 2023) can be sensitive to prompt templates (Wei et al., 2025) and stylistic biases (Feuer et al., 2025). Critically, to our knowledge, none of these has been validated against human similarity judgments for open-ended, interpretive tasks.

We introduce IDEAlign, a benchmarking paradigm that elicits expert similarity judgments via a simple pick-the-odd-one-out task. Given three annotations of the same source document, experts select the most dissimilar one along a specified, domain-relevant criterion (e.g., “what change to the student’s writing is being recommended?”). Aggregating many triplet decisions yields calibrated pairwise similarity scores without requiring absolute rating scales, leveraging the well-documented reliability of relative judgments (Laming, 2003; Jones and Alcock, 2012; Pollitt, 2012; Tarricone and Newhouse, 2016; Routh et al., 2023). Our triplet design follows prior comparative-judgment and “topic intruder/odd-one-out” work (Chang et al., 2009) and can be coupled with standard preference-aggregation models to obtain scales and ranks (Bradley and Terry, 1952). The same triplet template also appli es naturally to LLM-as-a-judge, enabling a direct comparison between human and model similarity judgments within a shared protocol.

Using IDEAlign, we then evaluate families of automated similarity measures: (i) lexical overlap (BLEU), (ii) cosine similarity from 16 embedding models with/without PCA post-processing, (iii) topic-distribution divergence via BERTopic and MALLET-LDA, and (iv) LLM-as-a-judge under three prompt formats (binary, continuous, and triplet). We validate each method by correlating its pairwise similarity rankings with the expert benchmark.

We study two education tasks where expert, idea-level interpretation matters: (1) assessing students’ mathematical reasoning from classroom transcripts and (2) providing in-line feedback to student essays. Across both settings, embedding- and topic-based metrics often mis-rank pairs in ways experts do not, suggesting sensitivity to confounders such as style and length. In contrast, prompting LLMs with the triplet (odd-one-out) format consistently improves alignment with expert judgments, yielding 9–30% higher rank correlations than traditional lexical and vector-based baselines.

Together, these results position IDEAlign as a practical foundation for evaluating whether LLMs “have the same ideas” as experts in open-ended annotation: (i) offering a reliable way to collect human similarity ground truth, and (ii) a validated path to scalable annotation once an LLM shows high agreement with experts.

2 Related Work

Comparing large language models to humans on open-ended tasks:

A growing number LLMs are now being used for open-ended, interpretive tasks, such as storytelling (Ismayilzada et al., 2025), news writing (Spangher et al., 2024; Muñoz-Ortiz et al., 2024), and explanation generation (Wiegreffe et al., 2022). Manually validating that LLMs generate ideas and interpretations similar to those of human experts is not feasible at scale.

Existing evaluations of LLMs in interpretive tasks typically focus on quantifiable features such as lexical diversity, response length, and grammar (Muñoz-Ortiz et al., 2024; Martínez et al., 2024) rather than content alignment with humans. Other approaches rely on humans assigning scores or giving preference labels according to specific criteria, such as helpfulness and creativity (Ismayilzada et al., 2025; Spangher et al., 2024; Wiegreffe et al., 2022).

MAUVE (Pillutla et al., 2021) introduces a novel approach for analyzing the divergence between distributions of human and LLM generated texts. However, it still relies on text embeddings to estimate distributions and does not disentangle confounders (e.g. writing style, tone, length) from the idea-level similarity which is central to our analysis. They also require thousands of samples from both LLMs and humans to approximate the distributions, which can limit the feasibility of analysis with small sample sizes.

Automated metrics for similarity:

There are many standard NLP metrics for text comparison, such as BLEU Papineni et al. (2002b) and ROUGE Lin (2004). However, their focus on lexical overlap fails to capture similarity in underlying ideas.

Vector-based similarity measures based on text embeddings like Word2Vec Ng and Abrecht (2015), BERT Devlin et al. (2019) have been proposed and further developed through methods like  Zhao et al. (2019); Zhang et al. (2020) and embedding models, including Sentence-BERT Reimers and Gurevych (2019), GPT-2 Radford et al. (2019), GTE Li et al. (2023), and proprietary models such as ada Greene et al. (2022) and cpt-text Neelakantan et al. (2022). Post-processing techniques (e.g., removing projections of the top principal components from word embeddings Mu et al. (2018) and keeping the top 2/32/3 of principal components Raunak et al. (2020)) are developed to improve performance on various NLP benchmarks including semantic similarity. However, it remains unclear whether these embeddings produce similarity scores aligned with human judgments. No single embedding model consistently dominates across NLP benchmarks Muennighoff et al. (2023), and Fabbri et al. (2021) report that many existing metrics correlate poorly with human judgments. This motivates a closer examination of automatic similarity measures and their alignment with human evaluations.

Alternatively, topic modeling methods such as LDA Blei et al. (2001) and BERTopic Grootendorst (2022) can be used to identify ideas expressed in annotations by different annotators (both humans and LLMs alike), and to quantify similarity based on the divergence of their topic distributions. Similar to embedding-based methods, each document is represented by a vector of topics and their corresponding frequencies. To measure (dis)similarity between any document pair in terms of their underlying topic distributions, any distributional divergence measure can be used. However, as our experimental results will show, topic modeling–based similarity measures can be sensitive to hyperparameters (e.g., the number of topics), which may cause topics to be defined too broadly or too narrowly, thus limiting meaningful comparison.

3 Setup

Given a source text, annotators (either LLMs or humans) generate interpretations or open-ended text responses, which we denote as A, B, C, etc. The goal is to compute the idea-level similarity for each document pair, Sim(A, B), Sim(B, C), and Sim(A, C), and to generate scores quantifying how similar each pair of annotators is to one another. This provides a framework for evaluating LLMs against humans even when human-generated responses vary and no single ground truth can be established.

4 Method

We first establish IDEAlign: a benchmarking method for eliciting expert similarity judgments via a pick-the-odd-one-out task. Then, we show how to use the human evaluation data to assess the alignment of automated similarity measures based on (1) lexical overlap, (2) vector-based representations (using cosine similarity of text embeddings and divergences of topic distributions), and (3) LLM-as-a-judge. Particularly, within the LLM-as-a-judge framework, we show how to apply the pick-the-odd-one-out protocol from IDEAlign to model evaluations.

4.1 IDEAlign: Benchmarking expert judgments via pick-the-odd-one-out task

A naive alternative to measuring idea-level similarity with expert humans is to ask them to provide continuous similarity ratings on a fixed scale. However, absolute judgments are cognitively difficult and may yield noisy, hard-to-calibrate labels when multiple annotators contribute. Prior work has therefore relied on relative judgments as an alternative to absolute scoring (Laming, 2003; Jones and Alcock, 2012; Pollitt, 2012; Tarricone and Newhouse, 2016; Routh et al., 2023) . Our task design builds on this line of work, including the “topic intruder/odd-one-out” paradigm introduced by  Chang et al. (2009). IDEAlign leverages relative human judgments through a pick-the-odd-one-out task and generates well-calibrated, continuous pairwise similarity scores by aggregating many triplet decisions.

Task protocol

In the pick-the-odd-one-out task, each evaluator provides a relative judgment over a group of three annotations by selecting the most dissimilar one according to a domain-specific criterion. We repeat this task with multiple evaluators across different triplets so that each annotation pair within a triplet is evaluated a sufficient number of times to yield reliable pairwise similarity scores when aggregated.

Aggregating triplet judgments

To enable comparisons with automated similarity measures, we convert triplet judgments into pairwise similarity scores. Suppose we want to compute a similarity score between AA and BB. For every triplet involving AA, BB, and a third annotation, we count the number of times either AA or BB is selected as the odd one out. Intuitively, the similarity score should be increased when AA and BB co-occur in a triplet without being selected, and decreased when either AA or BB is selected as the odd one. The more similar AA and BB are, the more likely the third annotation will be chosen as the odd one. Conversely, the more dissimilar AA and BB are, the more likely one of them will be chosen when compared against a third item. Based on this property, we define a scalar-valued similarity score by aggregating the triplet judgments as follows:

sim​(A,B)=Number of times neither ​A​ nor ​B​ is selected in a tripletTotal number of triplets containing both ​A​ and ​B\text{sim}(A,B)=\frac{\text{Number of times neither }A\text{ nor }B\text{ is selected in a triplet}}{\text{Total number of triplets containing both }A\text{ and }B}

 (1)

This score is computed for every annotation pair. We ensure that the denominator in Equation (1) exceeds a certain threshold for all pairs to ensure reliability. To satisfy this requirement while keeping the total number of triplet judgments manageable, we implement a prioritized sampling strategy when constructing triplets. Specifically, items that have appeared less frequently in previous triplets are given higher sampling priority, so that underrepresented pairs are more likely to be included in new triplets.

4.2 Lexical-based similarity

First, we consider lexical-based measures such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002a; Lin and Och, 2004), which compute n-gram overlap between two texts. To measure the similarity of AA and BB, we calculate BLEU with AA as the prediction and BB as the reference, and vice versa, then average the two scores. This ensures that the similarity score is invariant to the ordering of the pair. In our experiments, we use BLEU with a maximum n-gram order of 4.

4.3 Vector-based similarity

Under vector-based similarity, we consider two approaches to representing documents as vectors, from which pairwise similarity scores can be easily derived: (i) text embeddings and (ii) vectorized topic distributions.

Cosine similarity of text embeddings

For embedding-based similarity, we examine 16 models listed in Table 1, with and without PCA-based post-processing methods proposed by Mu et al. (2018) and Raunak et al. (2020). When the embedding model has a small context window, we split the annotation text into sentences, embed each sentence, and average the sentence embeddings into a single vector. When the model supports a longer context, we directly embed the full text. We then compute cosine similarity to measure the similarity between two embedded documents.

Divergence of vectorized topic distributions

Another way to represent documents as vectors is through the distribution of topics captured in each document. We first run topic modeling algorithms such as BERTopic (Grootendorst, 2022) and LDA (Blei et al., 2001), converting each document from its original text form into a vector of topic categories with corresponding densities based on how frequently words from each topic appear. For annotations AA and BB, we obtain the corresponding topic distribution vectors TAT_{A} and TBT_{B}. Instead of using cosine distance as a measure of dissimilarity, we define similarity as one minus the divergence between TAT_{A} and TBT_{B}. We use the Hellinger distance to measure divergence because it can accommodate zero values, though other divergence measures could also be used. In our experiments, we apply (i) BERTopic (Grootendorst, 2022) and (ii) the MALLET (McCallum, 2002) implementation of LDA (Blei et al., 2001)11 1 BERTopic is implemented with the BERTopic , UMAP , and HDBSCAN Python packages, while LDA is implemented using maria-antoniak/little-mallet-wrapper . Both are open-source packages. to identify topic clusters and obtain topic representations of each document. Details about the hyperparameters used in our case studies are provided in the appendix.

4.4 LLM-as-a-judge

One potential limitation of prior methods based on lexical features or text-to-vector representations is that such similarity measures cannot account for which dimensions of similarity should be prioritized in evaluation. For example, two documents may be similar in tone or length but differ in their underlying ideas. However, it is infeasible to specify such criteria for lexical or vector-based methods, as they are not designed for specific domains or evaluation criteria.

LLM-as-a-judge provides a promising alternative because the specific instructions for evaluating similarity can be easily encoded in prompts. However, prompting LLMs to produce reliable similarity scores is still not straightforward, as LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., 2023) can be sensitive to prompt templates (Wei et al., 2025) and stylistic biases (Feuer et al., 2025). To explore the capabilities of LLMs in similarity assessment, we experiment with three task types: (i) binary: binary evaluation with discrete outputs, (ii) continuous: binary evaluation with continuous scores, and (iii) triplet: triplet-based assessment using the pick-the-odd-one-out protocol from IDEAlign. For each pairwise assessment, we sample 10 responses and average the resulting scores. Below, we present the shared prompt used to describe the task, along with individual instructions for each approach.

Shared prompt: You are a helpful high school English Language Arts teaching assistant. Three teachers have provided feedback on a student’s essay. The student is instructed to write an essay to the prompt: {meta data about the essay topic}. Below are the pieces of feedback from each teacher.

  1. 1.

    Binary: Are the pieces of feedback similar in terms of the changes they suggest the student should make? Decide based on the content of the feedback, not the style, tone, or length of the notes. Respond with ##1## if they are similar, and ##0## if they are dissimilar.

  2. 2.

    Continuous: Generate a similarity score (in float) between 0 and 1. A value closer to 0 means the feedback is very dissimilar, and a value closer to 1 means the feedback is very similar. You can output any continuous number between 0 and 1 and format it as ##number##.

  3. 3.

    Triplet: Choose the feedback that is least like the other two based on what the teacher is asking the student to change in their writing. Do not evaluate based on the teacher’s tone. Focus only on the content of the feedback. Respond with ##A## if feedback A is most different, ##B## if feedback B is most different, and ##C## if feedback C is most different.

We experimented with four state-of-the-art LLMs: GPT-4.1 OpenAI et al. (2024), GPT-4o-mini, Claude 4 Sonnet Anthropic (2025), and Claude 3.5 Sonnet Anthropic (2024) to assess generalizability of the LLM-as-a-judge method.

4.5 Metric for evaluating alignment between model and human similarity

We follow prior work (Faruqui and Dyer, 2014; Raunak et al., 2020) in reporting the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (ρ\rho) between the similarity rankings produced by automated metrics and those by human experts. The value of ρ\rho ranges from -1 to 1, with 0 for no correlation and 1 for perfect correlation.

5 Case Studies in Education

We apply our methods to two educational tasks based on student mathematical reasoning and essay feedback. Our goal is to showcase the utility of our evaluation framework for answering questions like: “How do we compare LLM-generated ideas to those of domain experts on open-ended, interpretive tasks?"

5.1 Assessing students’ mathematical reasoning

Annotation process

Eleven expert math teachers were provided with four deidentified transcripts of 6-8th grade math lessons22 2 Classroom data was collected under an IRB for human subject research #75294 in which teachers, students, and student guardians consented to their participation. along with the text and purpose of the math problems on which students worked. These transcripts were collected from middle schools in a large urban public school district in California. Each transcript contained between 300-600 lines of student and teacher utterances. Annotators marked specific lines of student utterances from each transcript to answer the following questions: (1) What are students saying in the selected piece(s) of evidence? (2) What does this piece (or pieces) of evidence tell you about students’ understanding and/or progress towards the lesson’s purpose? We also prompted ChatGPT and Claude 3.5 Sonnet to complete the same task and included two outputs per model. The average annotation length is 139.38 words, with a maximum length of 556.

IDEAlign with experts

The dataset of open-ended transcript annotations was then labeled for relative similarity by 10 additional math educators using the interface in Fig. 3. This resulted in a total of 640 triplet comparisons which we used as benchmarks for evaluating automated measures. The recruited and compensated experts annotated and labeled only deidentified classroom transcript data.

5.2 Providing feedback to student writing

Annotation process

We used 18 middle and high school student essays from open-source datasets (Hamner et al., 2012), with in-line feedback comments written by 32 experienced English Language Arts (ELA) educators, collected in prior work Mah et al. (); Tan et al. (2024). We additionally prompted four state-of-the-art models (Chat GPT, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Deepseek-V2.5) to provide in-line feedback to help students revise their current essay based on the teacher’s suggestions. The average combined length of all feedback comments from a feedback provider was 142.98 words, with a maximum length of 477.

IDEAlign with experts

The dataset of 458 points was labeled by seven ELA teachers. Teachers used the web-based interface, where they were presented with triplets of deidentified feedback either generated by human experts, LLMs, or a mix of both, and instructed to identify the most different one based on the content focus of the substantive changes recommended, rather than the tone, mechanics or style of the comments.

The similarity data was labeled by expert math or ELA educators. One ELA educator had 5-6 years of experience, and the rest had 8 or more years of teaching experience in the U.S. Evaluators were compensated at an hourly rate of $50 for their expertise, and each expert contributed approximately 3-4 hours. Additional details about the recruitment process and the interface for both the annotation and the similarity labeling tasks are provided in the appendix D.3.

6 Results

We evaluate how different automated measures of similarity compare to expert judgments from IDEAlign, based on Spearman ranking correlation coefficients. Table 2 summarizes our key experimental findings from two educational domains: students’ math reasoning and essay feedback. Across both settings, embedding and topic-based metrics often misrank pairs in ways experts do not, suggesting sensitivity to confounders such as style and length. In contrast, prompting LLMs with the triplet (odd-one-out) format consistently improves alignment with expert judgments, yielding 9–30% higher rank correlations than traditional lexical and vector-based baselines.

6.1 How do existing metrics (lexical and vector-based) compare to experts?

Table 2 shows the poor alignment of embedding models with human evaluation, especially with the student reasoning data. Even with PCA-based post-processing of the text embeddings based on prior work (Mu et al., 2018; Raunak et al., 2020), no embedding-based metric achieves correlations higher than 0.2 with the reasoning data, and they only show marginal improvements. With the feedback data, the correlations decrease after post-processing, potentially due to information loss from dimension reduction as observed in  Raunak et al. (2020).

Topic modeling–based approaches show improvements over the cosine similarity of text embeddings, but they still fail to achieve higher than 0.6 correlation coefficients with experts in both tasks. We also observed that topic modeling is sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, such as the number of topics to identify, so the same topic modeling method can yield correlation coefficients varying from 0.1310.131 to 0.5180.518 based on the hyperparameters (full results in Table 9).

These results suggest that existing metrics may lead to claims about similarity that conflict with experts, as suggested by negative and near-zero correlations. Furthermore, the same metric may perform accurately in one task but not in the other, as shown by the large performance gap between the reasoning and the feedback data for some measures like MiniLM. Therefore, it is crucial to validate automated measures of similarity against a reliable set of human evaluations.

6.2 Do LLM evaluations show benefits with pick-the-odd-one-out task protocol?

Using LLM-as-a-judge offers a more accurate alternative to standard measures based on text embeddings or topic modeling. This may be because LLMs can contextualize more task instructions regarding the criteria used to assess similarity. Results in Table 3 show that LLM-as-a-judge significantly improves alignment with experts by 30% in the reasoning similarity task and 9% in the feedback similarity task, compared to the best-performing text embedding-based metrics. These benefits tend to be especially pronounced when using triplet assessments, compared to binary comparisons, and in newer models. Table 3 shows that all models, except Claude Sonnet 3.5 with the reasoning data, perform best when prompted with our proposed pick-the-odd-one-out template.

6.3 Do LLMs, like experts, apply domain knowledge in similarity judgments?

Including metadata about the math lesson or the student’s essay topic does not consistently improve the performance of LLM-as-a-judge as shown in Table 4. In fact, longer contexts actually hurt performance in all models except Sonnet 3.5. In contrast, human evaluators mentioned the usefulness of having contextual information to situate the student’s essay or the math discussion within the broader educational purpose. This suggests that LLMs likely lack the domain knowledge to incorporate additional context when evaluating educational data.

6.4 How sensitive are existing metrics to stylistic level perturbations?

We noticed a discrepancy between the annotations that the embedding models picked out as most different and what the human experts chose. We hypothesized this was due to the formal versus casual writing style. To probe the model failures, we selected two documents with the lowest average similarity scores and revised them to be more formal without changing the content. The original and modified texts are in the appendix E. Table 5 shows that the embedding similarities increased by 20–85% following the style change. We observed a similar but smaller increase with GPT-4.1, but Sonnet 4’s similarity dropped, suggesting that Sonnet may be sensitive to features other than the one targeted by our experiment.

6.5 How many expert similarity judgments are sufficient for reliable evaluation?

One natural question practitioners interested in our benchmarking method might ask is: “How many pick-the-odd-one-out tasks are necessary to reliably compare automated similarity measures with expert judgments?" This question is especially relevant in resource-constrained testing environments, as collecting expert (human) data is expensive. Different similarity tasks may exhibit varying amounts of variance in expert judgments: if experts disagree substantially, a larger dataset is needed, whereas if they mostly agree, even a smaller dataset can yield reliable comparisons with automated similarity measures.

To answer this question, we explore bootstrapping across different sample sizes as a guide for determining whether the current task dataset size is sufficient for drawing reliable ranking comparisons between human evaluations and automated measures. Based on ranking consistency (measured by Spearman correlation coefficients), we observe that at least 600 tasks are necessary for the reasoning data, while 300 tasks are sufficient for the feedback data to generate consistent rankings, with both achieving correlation values higher than 0.8 across bootstrapping runs. Since our evaluation dataset contains over 400 feedback data points and 600 reasoning task data points, we conclude that our current datasets are sufficient for the analysis. It is important to note that the required dataset size may vary depending on the inherent variance in human judgments for specific tasks. Therefore, we recommend that practitioners run this bootstrapping analysis to investigate ranking consistency across different task set sizes to to determine (1) whether more expert task data is needed, and (2) what would be an appropriate sample size for future tasks of a similar nature.

7 Discussion & Conclusion

As interest grows in evaluating LLM outputs to experts’ for open-ended tasks Spangher et al. (2024); Muñoz-Ortiz et al. (2024); Ismayilzada et al. (2025), we need analysis tools that go beyond surface-level features like word overlap, length, and style. For example, researchers might ask: “Do LLMs assess students’ reasoning or provide feedback like expert educators?” Answers to such questions can inform how we incorporate LLMs into assisting students and teachers.

We observe a gap in applying existing similarity metrics to open-ended, interpretive tasks, as they often emphasize stylistic and lexical features rather than conceptual alignment. Our style perturbation experiment shows that text embedding-based metrics can be easily manipulated to produce higher similarity without substantive content changes. On the other hand, LLM-as-a-judge using the IDEAlign protocol achieves a significant improvement in alignment with expert similarity judgments (a 9–30% increase compared to traditional lexical and vector-based methods). However, our empirical results that include metadata in the prompt template suggest that there is still room for improvement in applying domain knowledge to LLM judgment.

For NLP and social science researchers, clustering similar ideas and comparing emergent themes in annotations is a crucial but time-intensive step in analysis. Developing automated metrics that highlight similarities and differences in ideas at scale can support data analysis beyond LLM evaluations. Our experiments focus on two educational tasks, and we encourage future work to extend our analysis to other settings that also require domain expertise for similarity judgments.

Limitation

Defining dimensions of similarity with domain experts is crucial to our analysis. For instance, even within math education, the criteria for measuring similarity may vary depending on the downstream task and the data from which the annotations are generated. Therefore, collaborating with human experts is essential, though it can be expensive compared to fully automated evaluation pipelines.

In this paper, we focus on two educational tasks, assessing student math reasoning and providing essay feedback, but there are many other tasks, both within and beyond education that also require domain expertise to generate meaningful interpretations and measure similarity. While our method can be applied to various open-ended, interpretive text-generation tasks, our data and analysis regarding the appropriate human evaluation sample size and the performance of different automated metrics are limited to the specific tasks discussed in this paper. We selected these examples to demonstrate the utility of our evaluation framework, which can be applied more broadly.

Lastly, while LLM judges are promising, our experimental results suggest they still lack domain expertise, and prior work has questioned the reliability of their outputs Feuer et al. (2025). Therefore, we recommend validating any automated metrics, including LLM-as-a-judge, against human evaluations.

Ethical considerations

Math classroom transcript data was collected under an IRB for human subject research (approval number: 75294) in which teachers, students, and student guardians consented to their participation. The feedback data was collected in prior work Mah et al. (); Tan et al. (2024). Recruited and compensated experts for similarity assessments only used deidentified data.

Regarding the intended use of our method, we propose a benchmarking task for measuring the similarity of ideas as a scalable way to assess LLM-generated responses against those of expert humans. However, high similarity scores do not imply endorsing indiscriminate use of LLMs in education. Other social and educational risks of using LLMs in classrooms or to interact with students should be considered holistically, regardless of their idea-level similarity to human teachers.

Appendix B Hyperparameters for topic modeling and embedding post-processing

Topic modeling hyperparameters

We used BERTopic package for topic modeling, UMAP for dimension reduction, and HDBSCAN for clustering. The parameters for UMAP are: n neighbors = 3, n components = 100, min distance = 0, metric = cosine. The parameters for HDBSCAN are min samples = 1, metric = euclidean. We set the min cluster size of HDBSCAN as a tunable hyperparameter and enumerated between {2,3,..,15}\{2,3,..,15\}. The full result table with varying cluster sizes can be found in Table 9.

We used an open-sourced Python wrapper for MALLET implementation of LDA by maria-antoniak/little-mallet-wrapper. For both the math and the feedback domains, we enumerated the number of topics to find from {50,75,100,125,150}\{50,75,100,125,150\} and reported the results with varying topic number in Table 9. With the math data, LDA topic modeling could not find more than 125 unique topics.

Our experiments do not rely on GPU resources.

Appendix C Prompts for LLM evaluations

C.1 Pick-the-odd-one-out for the feedback data

You are a helpful high school English Language Arts teaching assistant. Three teachers have provided feedback on a student’s essay. The student is instructed to write an essay to the prompt: {meta data about the essay topic}. Below are the pieces of feedback from each teacher. Choose the feedback that is least like the other two based on what the teacher is asking the student to change in their writing. Do not evaluate based on the teacher’s tone. Focus only on the content of the feedback. Respond with ##A## if feedback A is most different, ##B## if feedback B is most different, and ##C## if feedback C is most different.

C.2 Pick-the-odd-one-out for the reasoning data

You are a helpful math assistant. Teachers were given a transcript of students working on a math lesson and this information about that lesson’s purpose: {meta data about the lesson}. Teachers were then asked to make notes about what students said in the transcript that would help them assess and/or advance student’s understanding toward the lesson purpose. These are the notes that three different teachers made about the transcript. Choose the set of notes that is least like the other two sets of notes.

C.3 Binary similarity assessment for the feedback data

Binary output

You are a helpful high school English Language Arts teaching assistant. Three teachers have provided feedback on a student’s essay. The student is instructed to write an essay to the prompt: {meta data about the essay topic}. Below are the pieces of feedback from each teacher. Are the pieces of feedback similar in terms of the changes they suggest the student should make? Decide based on the content of the feedback, not the style, tone, or length of the notes. Respond with ##1## if they are similar, and ##0## if they are dissimilar.

Continuous output

You are a helpful high school English Language Arts teaching assistant. Three teachers have provided feedback on a student’s essay. The student is instructed to write an essay to the prompt: {meta data about the essay topic}. Below are the pieces of feedback from each teacher. Are the pieces of feedback similar in terms of the changes they suggest the student should make? Decide based on the content of the feedback, not the style, tone, or length of the notes. Generate a similarity score (in float) between 0 and 1. A value closer to 0 means the feedback is very dissimilar, and a value closer to 1 means the feedback is very similar. You can output any continuous number between 0 and 1 and format it as ##number##.

C.4 Binary similarity assessment for the reasoning data

Binary output

You are a helpful math assistant. Teachers were given a transcript of students working on a math lesson and this information about that lesson’s purpose: {meta data about the lesson}. Teachers were then asked to make notes about what students said in the transcript that would help them assess and/or advance student’s understanding toward the lesson purpose. These are the notes that three different teachers made about the transcript. Are these notes similar in terms of the underlying ideas? Do not evaluate based on the teacher’s tone. Focus only on the content of the feedback. Respond with ##1## if they are similar, and ##0## if they are dissimilar.

Continuous output

You are a helpful math assistant. Teachers were given a transcript of students working on a math lesson and this information about that lesson’s purpose: {meta data about the lesson}. Teachers were then asked to make notes about what students said in the transcript that would help them assess and/or advance student’s understanding toward the lesson purpose. These are the notes that three different teachers made about the transcript. Are these notes similar in terms of the underlying ideas? Decide based on the content rather than the style, tone, or length of the notes. Generate a similarity score (in float) between 0 and 1. A value closer to 0 means the notes are very dissimilar, and a value closer to 1 means the notes are very similar. You can output any continuous number between 0 and 1 and format it as ##number##.

Appendix D Details about the educational tasks and data

D.1 Expert recruitment for annotation and labeling of the de-identified artifacts

We recruited expert ELA and math educators for labeling the similarity data through a graduate school of education alumni mailing list and snowball sampling based on teacher networks affiliated with the school of education. The recruited and compensated experts annotated and labeled only deidentified classroom transcript data. Annotators were compensated at an hourly rate of $50 for their expertise. Demographics of the expert labelers for the student reasoning data are: 4 White or Caucasian female, 2 Asian male, 1 Black or African American male, 1 White or Caucasian male, 1 Multi-racial female, and 1 Multi-racial prefer-not-to-say. Demographics of the expert labelers for the feedback data are: 4 White or Caucasian female, 1 White or Caucasian male, 1 Hispanic or Latine female, and 1 Black or African American female. One ELA educator has 5-6 years of teaching experience and the rest have 8 or more years of experience. They are all based in the U.S.

D.2 Data accessibility

We share the full annotations for the math reasoning data which we collected under an IRB for human subject research, and a subset of the feedback collected by Mah et al. (); Tan et al. (2024) who consented to sharing a subset of their feedback data to help the reviewers understand the similarity evaluation tasks. The data files are organized as: data which includes the expert and LLM annotations, metadata which includes metadata about the math lesson or the student’s writing assignment, tasker2task mapping which contains a mapping of the expert IDs to the task IDs, and task2annotation mapping, which contains a mapping of the task IDs used during the similarity evaluations to the annotation texts. similarity judgments include the labels from the pick-the-odd-one evaluations linked to each tasker ID. Aggregated similarity scores are in human-eval scores.

    Original document #1: Students are debating if 10x10 is 100 or 20., Ultimately they say that it is 100, and that 10x10x10 is 1000. Then they state that 1000 times 100 is ‘one thousand one hundred‘, That 10010^{0} is 10., Students are counting 10s by 1’s, 2’s and 3’s. The number that they count is the exponent.

  • •

    After style change #1: Students are debating if 10 multiplied by 10 should be 100 or 20. They conclude that it should be 100. Similarly, they discuss that 10 multiplied by 10, multiplied by another 10 is a thousand. Then, they reach the conclusion that 1000 times 100 is ’one thousand and one hundred.’, Students argue that 10 to the power of 0 is 10., Students are counting the powers of 10.

  • •

    Original document #2: Student debate over 10 raised to 2 being 10 times 2 = 20 and 10 times 10 = 100., That after expanding the expressions you would have to add instead of multiplying.

  • •

    After style change #2: Students are debating whether 10 to the power of 2 should be interpreted as 10×2=2010\times 2=20 or as 10×1010\times 10 = 100., Afterwards, students are discussing whether the correct step is to add rather than multiply.
